children: By Liz Young
The Trump administration is escalating its crackdown on immigrant truck drivers.

The WSJ's Mariah Timms and Esther Fung report that the Department of Homeland Security and the Transportation Department are demanding licensing data across the U.S. as they search for what they say is a rash of drivers with improper certifications.
The administration has forced the closure of some commercial-driving training schools and apprehended drivers who have commercial driver's licenses but may be in the country illegally.

U.S. officials this week said they are intensifying those efforts. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced his agency has shut down nearly 300 driving schools that he said were failing to train drivers properly.

Immigration officials have been setting up stings on interstate highways for months, sweeping up hundreds of migrants who allegedly are in the country illegally. The efforts have tightened trucking capacity nationwide, in turn pushing up pricing after a yearslong slump in demand.
Quote of the Day
Economy & Trade

America's retailers are feeling jolly heading into the busy fall shopping season. The WSJ's Sarah Nassauer and Theo Francis write that retailers say consumers are spending even as they navigate higher fuel prices and long-term inflation. Tariff refunds are also helping fuel heftier sales and earnings.

Discount seller Dollar General posted a fifth consecutive quarter of higher traffic. Electronics retailer Best Buy said shoppers were buying up computers, TVs and AI-enabled glasses. And Target logged higher sales, profit and a benefit from tariff refunds as shoppers purchased more toys, food and beauty products.

Still, the reports of robust spending run counter to some recent economic indicators. Government retail-sales data for July showed overall softening, and a widely watched measure of consumer confidence slipped in August as consumers fretted about future economic conditions.
Number of the Day
The transportation cost index in the August Logistics Managers' Index report, up 3.1 percentage points from July and the fourth out of five months the measure of freight transport costs expanded.
E-Commerce

Shein became one of the world's largest fashion retailers by winning over shoppers with $3 T-shirts and $10 jeans. The company that pioneered ultrafast fashion now faces a question of what comes next.

The WSJ's Stu Woo writes that Shein made a subdued stock-market debut this week. Shares fell as much as 10% on the Hong Kong exchange before rebounding close to the initial public offering price, leaving the company with a valuation far below its peak in 2022.

The company grew using a responsive supply chain that allowed it to churn out styles in days instead of weeks. It took advantage of a trade exemption that allowed it to ship orders directly from overseas warehouses to American doorsteps duty free.
But the end of that provision last year has hit Shein hard. Sales growth slowed to 8% last year after rising 21% from 2023 to 2024.
